config_verbatim:
# The over-chunked end of the chunking sweep.
#
# Three configs share the nomic-embed-text model and vary only the chunker,
# so the difference between them is chunking and nothing else:
#
#   native-wholedoc      capped-whole-5000   1.06 chunks/node
#   redstring-native     boundary-preference 1.14 chunks/node
#   native-sliding1k     sliding-1000-500    ~1.94 chunks/node (estimated)
#
# A 1000-character window advancing 500 puts every position of a long
# document into two chunks. Deliberately aggressive: the question is whether
# chunking helps or hurts, and one point either side of the current default
# is what makes the answer a direction rather than an anecdote.
#
# Two things to hold in mind when reading the result:
#
#  - 86% of this corpus (111,001 of 129,575 documents) is under 1000
#    characters and comes through whole under every one of the three. The
#    sweep can only move the 14% long tail.
#  - SlidingWindowChunker emits exactly one fully-redundant final chunk per
#    document over the window size (for 2600 chars: [2000,2600) then
#    [2100,2600)). That is ~18.6k of the ~250.7k chunks here. It is waste,
#    not corruption -- the text is real -- but it means chunk COUNT for this
#    config overstates distinct coverage by about 7%.
#
# Shares one chunk table with the other two native configs -- same
# model, same dimension, same prefixes, ADR 0002 and 0043 satisfied --
# isolated from each other by tenant_id.
name: native-sliding1k
dataset: prime
split: test-0.1
chunker: sliding-1000-500
embeddings: Nemotron-3-Embed-1B
dimension: 2048
aggregation: max
agent: dense
k: 20

# nomic-embed-text-v1.5 is asymmetric: it was trained with these exact task
# prefixes and expects them at inference. Omitting them is silent -- the
# vectors are well-formed and score plausibly, just worse than the model can
# do -- which is why every nomic config states them rather than relying on a
# default.
document_prefix: "passage: "
query_prefix: "query: "
